title: Part 1
text: A fish the size of a shoe wore a shell of bone from nose to belly. Why would it carry that much weight?

title: Part 2
text: Sacabambaspis was a jawless fish that swam in Ordovician seas roughly 450 million years ago.
nxt: Its front half was covered in two large bony shields, one on the back and one on the belly. Behind them, a flexible tail drove it forward.

title: Part 3
text: The armor was made of a very old kind of bone tissue called aspidin. It had layers, like a sandwich.
nxt: A thin layer lay at the base, a spongy layer sat in the middle, and a hard, ridged layer sat on top.

title: Part 4
text: And the armor also held a sensing system. Under a microscope, the surface of the armor shows grooves and pits.
nxt: In early fishes like this one, such grooves held a sense organ, called the lateral line, that picks up vibrations in the water.

title: Part 5
text: So what was it afraid of? We do not know for sure.
nxt: One idea is that large hunters of that time, such as the big sea scorpions called eurypterids and shelled cephalopods, made armor worth having.

title: Part 7
text: Then armor appeared, and with it came a new idea about bone.
nxt: A popular hypothesis is that bone started outside the body, as a coat, and only later moved inward to become the skeleton.
